[2404] REGIONAL INTEGRATION OF THE DEFENSE INDUSTRY The Statute of the South American Defense Council approved by the Heads of State of UNASUR in Santiago (Chile) in December 2008 establishes among its specific objectives the promotion of exchange and cooperation in the field of the defense industry

[2405] The autonomous and cooperative dimension of Argentina's defensive positioning finds in the areas of research, development, and production a genuine strategic option for the development of technological and industrial projects that contribute to deepening the process of regional integration

[2409] Chapter XVIII Education for defense includes the processes of training, capacity building and improvement of personnel (civil and military) of the Ministry of Defense and the Armed Forces

[2410] In the case of military personnel (officers and non-commissioned officers), it covers their training from the initial phase in basic institutes, their training and further development in specific War Colleges and the Joint War College, and the establishment of joint courses in different specialties

[2411] In the case of civilian personnel, educational policy addresses the academic offering through the National Defense School and other institutes

[2412] A specific chapter is the contribution to the training of adolescents in secondary or middle education establishments that operate within the orbit of the Armed Forces

[2413] the military high schools

[2414] In Argentina there are three basic officer training schools: - The National Military College, for the Army, - The Naval Military School, for the Navy, and - The Military Aviation School, for the Air Force; and four non-commissioned officer schools: - The Army Non-Commissioned Officer School, - The Navy Non-Commissioned Officer School, - The Air Force Non-Commissioned Officer School, - The “Ezeiza” Training Institute of the Air Force

[2415] Officer training lasts four to five years, while non-commissioned officer training lasts one to two and a half years

[2416] The basic education currently received by future officers and non-commissioned officers is integrated into Argentina's public higher education system

[2417] For this reason, cadets graduate with a military rank: second lieutenant (Army), midshipman (Navy) or ensign (Air Force) and with a university degree (Conduction and Operational Management, in the Army; Administration of Naval Resources for Defense, in the Navy; and Air and Aerospace Systems, in the Air Force

[2418] Candidates who graduate from non-commissioned officer schools do so with a military rank, a high school diploma, and a non-university technical degree

[2419] After graduation from the establishments where basic training is provided, the cycle or period of improvement and training begins

[2420] In the case of the Army, junior officers (from second lieutenant to captain) first attend the Weapons School, in Campo de Mayo, where they take short courses

[2421] As chief officers (major and lieutenant colonel) they take the General Staff courses at the Army War College

[2422] Junior non-commissioned officers also undergo their initial training at the aforementioned Weapons School

[2423] In the case of the Navy, junior officers (from midshipman to lieutenant) first complete a basic specialization course at the Naval Officers' School, and five years later return to the same establishment to complete a tactical-level course

[2424] Both officers and non-commissioned officers take specific courses for the different units at the School of Techniques and Tactics

[2425] Chief officers (corvette and frigate captains) complete the Command and Staff course at the Naval War College

[2426] In the Air Force, junior officers (from second lieutenant to captain) undergo their initial training in various areas according to their rank

[2427] Air Force officers complete this course through the Joint Basic Military Aviator Course (CBCAM) at the Military Aviation School

[2428] Technical officers complete their advanced training at the Aeronautical Engineering and Electronic Engineering faculties of the Aeronautical University Institute

[2429] As for those in the General Class, they receive further training at various establishments according to their specialty: the Aeronautical University Institute, the Exploration and Reconnaissance School, the Defense Electronics School, and the Anti-Aircraft Artillery School

[2430] The Higher Air War College offers advanced training courses to junior officers (from second lieutenant to captain) of the General Staff Assistant and to chief officers (major and vice-commodore) of the General Staff

[2431] Air Force non-commissioned officers complete training and improvement courses throughout their careers as a condition of promotion

[2432] Armed Forces officers and non-commissioned officers specializing in intelligence take joint training and advanced courses at the Armed Forces Intelligence Institute, which is run by the Joint Chiefs of Staff

[2433] Finally, the final stage is the Joint War College, which trains Armed Forces Staff officers

[2434] The courses taught there are at the postgraduate level

[2435] Level I is for chief officers and is called the Joint Staff and Planning Course, while Level II is for senior officers (from colonel, commodore, and captain) and is called the Joint Strategy and Senior Leadership Course

[2436] At the time of publication of this book, both are in the process of being accredited by the National Commission for University Evaluation and Accreditation (CONEAU) to achieve postgraduate status, in the first case as a Specialization Program and in the second as a Master's Program

[2437] The Armed Forces' university institutes offer undergraduate, graduate, and postgraduate programs in various disciplines and are the link between the Defense Education Subsystem and the National Education System

[2438] These institutes, located within each force, maintain functional subordination to the Ministry of Defense through the Undersecretariat of Training

[2439] The institutes do not have government autonomy, nor economic-financial self-sufficiency in the sense granted by the Higher Education Law to national university institutions. The Aeronautical University Institute (IUA) was integrated into the National University System in 1971 and was definitively categorized as a University Institute and incorporated into the National University system in 1995 with the restrictions on autonomy and government inherent to the category

[2440] In 1990, the Army Institute of Higher Education (IESE) was created to house, along with the university academic units (the National Military College, and the Higher War and Higher Technical Schools), the six military high schools, the "Dr. Dámaso Centeno" Military Social Institute, the "Sergeant Cabral" Non- Commissioned Officers School and the Army Distance Education Service (SEADEA). IESE has the role of coordinating the institutes that make up its structure and acting as a communication link between them and the Ministries of Education and Defense

[2441] The Naval University Institute (INUN) was created a year later, in 1991, and initially consisted of three academic units—the Naval Military School, the Naval Officers' School, and the Naval War College—later incorporating the National Nautical School and the School of Marine Sciences

[2442] The Higher Education Law (Law 24.521) was sanctioned in 1995, in its art

[2443] established that "institutions established under the provisions of Article 16 of Law 17,778, which are categorized as university institutes by this law, shall establish their system of government in accordance with their own institutional frameworks, and the rules on autonomy and government of national university institutions provided for in this law shall not apply to them

Its mission is to provide interdisciplinary, university-level education to students from the public and private sectors within a framework of integration among the community's various sectors. It also conducts studies and research on strategy, strategic planning, and national defense

[2454] This latest postgraduate program is the result of the signing of a framework agreement for academic cooperation and exchange between the National University of Tres de Febrero and the Ministry of Defense, the purpose of which is to foster mutual cooperation in the development of training programs and activities

[2455] The professional specialization of a military career also presupposes the strengthening of civic awareness and public service

[2456] Therefore, specific technical-military training is integrated with the general training of government officials and is updated with the official education system

[2457] The organization, content and teaching practices constitute a subsystem within the National Education System

[2458] Thus, the Ministry of Defense coordinates guidelines with the Ministry of Education, the National Commission for University Evaluation and Accreditation, and other relevant organizations

[2459] This refers to both teaching and learning methods and the appropriateness of the teaching role at each level (forms of sociability and relationships between teachers and instructors with students, cadets, or applicants

[2460] Reception ceremony for Army officers at the Military College

[2461] Likewise, and in accordance with these guidelines, higher education in the field of national defense includes, as one of its substantive functions, research and transfer activities

[2462] Consequently, undergraduate and graduate education must be aligned with specific scientific and technological development, meeting the quality and relevance assessment criteria established by the National System of Science, Technology, and Innovation. The real possibility of such integration is closely linked to the modernization of the educational offerings of the Armed Forces' university institutes

[2463] and the incorporation of quality criteria in management

[2464] On the other hand, the strategic importance of human resource training in defense also lies in the fact that while the incorporation of a modern weapons system can take between three and five years, the development of the skills, abilities, and knowledge required by operating and technical personnel requires longer periods of time, and can even be measured in decades

[2465] Finally, for specific military education, joint training has been established as one of the key principles, with the aim of establishing the basis for functional coordination between forces, enhancing their capabilities, and effectively coordinating procedures, leading to greater operational effectiveness and efficiency

[2466] THE TRANSFORMATION OF THE DEFENSE EDUCATION SYSTEM In 1998, the Armed Forces Restructuring Law established the need to make the military education system compatible with the national educational structure

[2467] However, the lack of regulations meant that by the middle of the first decade of the new century, comprehensive actions to train military professionals as full citizens and specialized public servants had still not been initiated

[2468] The training of civil society and raising awareness on the issue were also delayed subjects

[2469] In a context of political disinterest, the set of military educational institutions was diversified without any organizing criteria

[2470] This generated a chaotic dynamic where each of the Armed Forces

[2471] developed its own components, without any relationship or articulation with its peers and disconnected from the National Education System

[2472] Despite the progress made in extending a university degree to second lieutenants, midshipmen, and second lieutenants in the mid-1990s, the absence of precise guidelines to guide this process further undermined the academic excellence of these certifications

[2473] National Law 25.467/2001, Law on Science, Technology and Innovation

[2474] National Law

[2475] In order to correct the set of inconsistencies that had led to a distortion in the training and instruction of military personnel and civilians in the field of defense, a process of regulatory, organizational, and curricular transformation was promoted, essentially an institutional modernization

[2476] A precursor to this transformation was the debate generated in 2004 by the project "National Defense in the Democratic Agenda

[2477] This initiative addressed the educational issue and allowed for the development of a first framework of guiding ideas, which was processed and systematized in 2006, following the creation of an Advisory Council for the Reform of Armed Forces Education. This council's mandate was to evaluate, contribute experiences, recommendations, and other complementary perspectives to the training and development process of the Armed Forces

[2478] and of all the human resources of national defense

[2479] The transformation of the defense education subsystem revolved around the following axes: - The creation of a specialized political leadership body

[2480] The creation of an educational body for joint higher education

[2481] The establishment of joint basic courses in various specialties

[2482] Updating the curricula of basic and higher education institutes

[2483] The promotion of complementarity between the university institutes of the Armed Forces and the National University System

[2484] The design of training programs for civilians for defense

[2485] THE CREATION OF A SPECIALIZED INSTANCE OF POLITICAL LEADERSHIP Since the restoration of democracy and until the middle of the first decade of the 21st century, the Ministry of Defense had not developed an organic body at the political level with responsibility for the leadership of the defense education subsystem

[2486] The need for such a framework had not been imperative in the context of delegative management, but it became imperative as soon as it was decided to assume, with a systemic approach, the direction and control of military education policy from the Ministry of Defense

[2487] With this rationale, the Undersecretariat of Training was created in 2007, assigning it the responsibility of assisting in the formulation of teaching, training, and capacity building policies for national defense at all levels, and of participating in the direction and coordination of the operation of the Armed Forces' educational establishments, managing relations with other countries, institutions, and international organizations, and assisting in the design of policies for the training of civilian defense personnel. Under its jurisdiction are the National Defense School and the General Directorate of University Institutes of the Armed Forces

[2488] The Undersecretariat is responsible for intervening in the formulation of training and development policies for the Armed Forces, establishing standards and methodological guidelines consistent with the State's modernization guidelines, and for supervising, evaluating, and certifying ongoing training provided by the corresponding educational institutions of the Armed Forces

[2489] It also participates in the formulation and monitoring of the execution of study plans and programs and is responsible for the coordination between the University Institutes of the Armed Forces and the policies of the Ministry of Defense and the Joint Chiefs of Staff of the Armed Forces, as well as the integration of the university institutes of the Armed Forces

[2490] among themselves and with the National Education System

[2491] THE CREATION OF AN EDUCATIONAL BODY FOR JOINT HIGHER EDUCATION The Joint War College (ESGC), created in 2006, constitutes one of the most important institutes within the framework of the defense educational subsystem

[2492] It is responsible for providing training to senior officers and commanders to address the challenges that arise within the framework of joint military action

[2493] National Defense in the Democratic Agenda The "National Defense in the Democratic Agenda" project was launched in 2003 by decision of the National Executive Branch, with the aim of promoting the participation of civil society, Parliament, and political parties in the development of new defense policies and new models of military organization

[2494] In this context, the Ministry of Defense, with support from UNDP, promoted workshops with specialists, academics, defense-related non-governmental organizations, and international organizations to discuss and generate proposals regarding national defense policy and the role of the armed forces in consolidating democracy

[2495] The process was divided into three stages

[2496] Initially, an academic report was prepared as a result of the working and discussion panels

[2497] In a second stage, this information was used as discussion material in academic circles across the country through the creation of a virtual forum for consultation and debate, and through plenary sessions held at universities, study centers, and other relevant institutions

[2498] Finally, a participatory discussion process was launched, through workshops and seminars, and presentations by international experts convened for this purpose

[2499] This stage resulted in the development of the final document, which was submitted to the Executive Branch and the National Congress for subsequent publication

[2502] Following a series of actions required for its organic and functional establishment, the ESGC was inaugurated in early 2007 and began its activities with the delivery of the Joint Staff and Planning Course

[2503] Through a subsequent evaluation process, it was deemed necessary to reform and restructure the curriculum at both levels the school offers

[2504] Likewise, in 2009, a process of review and redefinition of the curricula was launched with a view to better coordinating training and aligning the final stage of systematic officer education with the standards of the National University System

[2505] To this end, the two courses offered by the School—the Joint Staff and Planning Course (for senior officers of the rank of major and equivalent) and the Joint Strategy and Higher Leadership Course (for senior officers and chiefs of the rank of colonel and lieutenant colonel and equivalent)—were redesigned as postgraduate, specialization, and master's programs, respectively, and presented in 2010 for accreditation by the National Commission for University Evaluation and Accreditation

[2506] The first course addresses training in the functions of the Joint and Combined Staffs and the development of command aptitude and analytical and communication skills, providing resources for military administration and leadership with a modern and comprehensive view of the problems posed by joint military action

[2507] In the second course, training is geared toward senior leadership of the Armed Forces

[2508] providing knowledge to perform positions in joint or combined staffs

[2509] Considering the dynamics of conflicts, it also includes preparation for integrating multidisciplinary teams and is aimed at achieving the best aptitude to meet the requirements imposed by national defense policy

[2510] Along with training senior officers at the highest academic and military levels, the Joint War College also aims to promote, coordinate, and develop research—with corresponding strategic analysis—on national, regional, and international realities in order to advise the highest levels of national political decision-making on matters of defense and international security, integrating and fostering broad, democratic, and pluralistic participation

[2511] The Armed Forces Educational Center (CEFA) Taking into account the positive results identified from the operation of the Army War College and the Joint War College in the same physical location, the Ministry of Defense evaluated the project of bringing together all the War Colleges on the same premises

[2512] Indeed, aside from the overall increase in efficiency resulting from the provision and use of common services and spaces, it was confirmed that the increased density of interaction between officers from different forces allows for the enhancement of joint higher education

[2513] This important building infrastructure will house, starting in 2012, the Army War College, the Joint War College—both currently located on the site—the Navy's Naval War College, the Air Force's Air War College, and the Armed Forces Intelligence Institute

[2514] Once completed, the CEFA course is expected to have the following capacities: Total capacity for 868 students

[2517] Two amphitheaters with capacity, one for 95 people and the other for

[2521] ESTABLISHMENT OF JOINT BASIC COURSES IN VARIOUS SPECIALITIES In the last decade, actions have been implemented to enhance the joint training and development of military personnel

[2522] Joint courses have proven to be a fundamental tool not only from a technical and operational perspective but also from a cultural perspective

[2523] The fact that personnel from one force live together for an extended period alongside members of other forces generates interaction and mutual understanding that will prove decisive in crisis situations

[2524] The following graph shows the evolution of the number of courses from 1999 to 2010, grouped into three categories: theoretical, in which knowledge is taught only in the classroom; operational, in which intensive theoretical instruction in tactics and techniques is provided and operational activities are carried out in the field; and mixed, in which theory is taught and then a practical examination of the content is carried out in the classroom or office

[2525] Navy tactical divers

[2526] The trend toward growth in joint courses is a consequence of the maturity achieved in consolidating the operational requirements of the three armed forces

[2527] which allows for better use of resources and greater synergy, both in the training and joint military operations stages. The following graph shows the evolution of the number of students trained in joint courses

[2532] OPERATIONAL COURSES These are some of the most important joint operational courses that have been implemented to date: Joint Command Training Course (CCCDOS) This joint course was created in 1996 with the aim of unifying the training of cadres – officers and non-commissioned officers – in the special aptitude of commands for the three Armed Forces

[2533] Since 2000, it has been implemented biannually during even-numbered years

[2534] Joint Basic Military Aviator Course (CBCAM) This course is taught at the Military Aviation School (EAM) of the Argentine Air Force

[2535] Since its approval in 2006, it has allowed for the unification of basic training courses for military aviators (fixed-wing aircraft pilots), taking advantage of the EAM's remaining capabilities

[2536] The Joint Chiefs of Staff exercises functional control of the course and the Air Force has operational control of its execution

[2537] The implementation of this course has generated a culture of convergence and complementarity, as well as the professional and personal integration of flight instructors and students from the three Forces

[2538] Joint Helicopter Pilot Course (CCPHEL) Like the previous course, since 2009 the CCPHEL centralized the training of helicopter pilots from the three Armed Forces

[2539] in one place: the Argentine Army Aviation School

[2540] The purpose of the CCPHEL is to train future pilots in common helicopter operating techniques and procedures through standardization and the transfer of knowledge and experience from instructors from all three forces

[2541] Upon graduation, military personnel receive helicopter pilot certification, which allows them to continue with the necessary specialization according to the specific mission of each force

[2542] Joint Basic Course for Military Paratroopers (CBCPAM) Created in early 2010, this course is taught at the Paratroopers and Commandos School of the Army's 4th Paratrooper Brigade, and its purpose is to provide joint training that qualifies personnel for their launch from aircraft in flight

[2543] The course is implemented by the Argentine Army's Education and Doctrine Command, while the Joint Chiefs of Staff exercises functional control

[2544] Among its benefits is the compatibility of the operational needs of the three Armed Forces

[2545] This has prevented the dispersion and overlapping of efforts in the training of future military paratroopers; standardized procedures in educational, operational, and security matters; and, at the logistical level, it has led to the adoption of consolidated requirements that meet the demands of the three components of the military instrument and the resulting improvement in interoperability

[2546] Joint Basic Military Diving Course (CBCBUM) Considering that the Army and Navy developed specific courses for the training of their military divers, while the Air Force did so in institutes of other national State agencies, in 2010 it was decided to take advantage of the idle services and infrastructure of the Argentine Navy's Submarine and Diving School, in order to teach there a single basic course that would respond to the operational requirements of divers for the three Armed Forces

[2547] The CBCBUM provides the initial and basic knowledge and skills for this specialty, in addition to serving as a multiplying factor by generating greater practice and adaptation of joint military doctrine, the logistical compatibility of equipment and systems, the standardization of procedures and tactics to the extent that specificity allows, and, fundamentally, developing enriching interaction between personnel with the Military Diver specialty belonging to the three military forces

[2548] Likewise, the following operational courses are imminent to be established: - Joint Air Defense Course - Joint Search and Rescue Course - Joint Radar Operators Course - Joint Combat Pilots Course - Joint Transport Pilots Course - Joint Sea Survival Course for Air Crews - Joint Wheeled Armored Vehicle Operators Course - Joint Amphibious Operations Course THEORETICAL AND MIXED COURSES Among the joint theoretical and mixed courses currently being taught are the following: Joint Military Instructor Training Course (CCFIM) Designed and taught by the Undersecretariat of Training of the Ministry of Defense –in coordination with the seven training institutes for officers and non-commissioned officers of the Armed Forces– it promotes the integration of normative, ethical and legal principles in the resolution of complex situations and defines a model for the transmission of knowledge, skills and practices in the basic military training of cadets and aspirants

[2549] Joint Military Airworthiness Courses (CCAM) In support of the General Directorate of Joint Military Airworthiness (DIGAMC), an organic entity of the Joint Staff that is the enforcement authority in matters of joint military airworthiness, a series of courses related to functions, activities and tasks inherent to said subject were established, which are attended by military and civilian personnel with capabilities and qualifications in the technical aeronautical area of the Ministry of Defense

[2550] Joint Antarctic Course (JAC) This course was created to cover the training of members of the three Armed Forces who are annually selected to serve as members of the Antarctic base crews

[2551] Given the specificities and obligations arising from the legislation of the Antarctic Treaty System, and the interaction with other national and international organizations involved in this activity, it was appropriate to unify the comprehensive and joint training of personnel who will serve in Antarctica, without prejudice to the complementary courses that each Force must provide, addressing specific operational needs and requirements

[2552] Joint Courses on Mine Action and Humanitarian Demining (CCAMYDH) Considering that everything related to "antipersonnel mines" and "humanitarian demining" is the primary responsibility of the Ministry of Defense, the need to establish the political and strategic criteria to guide these areas of action was assessed

[2553] Following a thorough analysis process, a joint training plan was established for officers, non-commissioned officers, and civilian personnel assigned to or potentially involved in mine action and humanitarian demining activities, both nationally and within the framework of participation in international organizations and military peacekeeping operations

[2554] JOINT CIVIL DEFENSE COURSES (CCDC) These courses were established to plan the execution and supervision of joint training related to civil protection activities taught within the scope of the Joint Staff of the Armed Forces

[2555] These are courses related to the functions, activities, and tasks inherent to civil protection and crisis management in disaster situations. They are aimed at both military and civilian personnel of agencies under the Ministry of Defense, as well as other national actors or jurisdictions (governmental or non-governmental organizations) that have a direct or indirect relationship with these activities. Joint Courses for Peacekeeping Operations (CCOMP). All joint courses related to peacekeeping operations are developed within the jurisdiction of the Argentine Joint Training Center for Military Peace Operations (CAECOPAZ) with the aim of training military and civilian personnel, both Argentine and from friendly countries, and joint contingents that are organized to participate in peacekeeping missions under the mandate of the United Nations

[2556] Joint Intelligence Courses (CCI) All intelligence-related courses are taught at the Armed Forces Intelligence Institute (IIFA), created in 2000 to cover the subject in a comprehensive manner that cuts across all components of the military instrument

[2557] The following theoretical and mixed courses are also imminent: - Joint Communications Course - Joint Operational Analyst Course - Joint Logistics Course - Joint Field Health Course - Joint Electronic Warfare Course

[2558] Updating the curricula of basic and higher education institutes. The review of curricular proposals and the establishment of a set of subjects for basic humanistic training was another axis of the transformation process

[2559] Aimed at officers and non-commissioned officers, the initiative aimed to consolidate the development of a military ethos founded on the affirmation of republican citizenship and military professionalism; to strengthen the legal and ethical training necessary for adequate performance as public servants and military professionals; and to provide training in the foundations and practice of public service through the study of fundamental knowledge from sociology, political science, law, and public administration, enabling a broad and diverse understanding of the changes characterizing the contemporary world

[2560] Likewise, the entry requirements and formats for submitting core subjects and courses were unified

[2561] The reform of the entry requirements resulted in a process of federalizing the registration process for applicants to officer and non-commissioned officer training institutes; and reforms to the entry and retention requirements for the Armed Forces

[2562] aimed at consolidating equal opportunities in access to a military career

[2563] Regarding the formats for presenting subjects, a uniform model was designed for their presentation at university institutes within the scope of national defense, analogous to that of the National University System, to allow for adequate supervision by the Ministry of Defense

[2564] Regarding uniformity of criteria in core subjects, a common curriculum was established for officer and non-commissioned officer training institutes, and common subjects were incorporated into the entrance courses for the training institutes of the three forces

[2565] This uniform approach aimed to strengthen joint action and, in addition, to train future cadres as military citizens and public officials

[2566] Another aspect of the transformation has been the development of a knowledge transfer model for training cadets and candidates for the Armed Forces

[2567] Through the training of military instructors, aimed at increasing their preparedness and unifying the criteria governing their actions, in order to achieve higher quality results and, at the same time, promote a comprehensive understanding of the common military profession of the Armed Forces

[2568] Promotion of complementarity between military university institutes and the national university system. Within the framework of the transformation process, the university institutes of the Armed Forces

[2569] They are making progress in their internal and external coordination: - Internal coordination refers to the implementation of measures that help generate cooperative and integrative relationships between academic activities, programs, study plans and research projects among the three university institutes

[2570] They seek to generate consensus for the integration of interests and common areas of knowledge without detriment to the activities or content necessarily specific to each Force

[2571] External coordination means promoting greater integration of institutes with the National University System through organic links with public or private universities, scientific and technological organizations, and other government departments, in order to avoid "inbreeding"; to offer their specific capabilities to the entire scientific community and society at large, while also benefiting from the generation and circulation of knowledge within civil society

[2572] In this regard, teams have been established to coordinate joint research, standardize language training, design inter-institutional postgraduate programs, develop a joint proposal for the future law regulating teaching within the system, and integrate joint actions for teacher development

[2573] In this regard, training sessions for teachers and instructors at various institutes have been prioritized, aimed at optimizing the implementation of the curriculum reform through both theoretical and didactic updates

[2574] The design of training programs for civilians for national defense The training of civilians for defense constitutes another fundamental axis in strengthening the capacity of civilian government of national defense policy

[2575] “There aren't many people in academia involved in defense issues yet

[2576] We believe they need to get involved because we also understand that defense has a multidisciplinary approach and that it has, and has had, a very important role in many countries in the development of science and technology and in generating important innovations

[2577] Arturo Somoza (Rector of UNCUYO) at the National Seminar on the 2010 White Paper on Defense “National Defense in Bicentennial Argentina,” National University of Cuyo, Mendoza, August

[2578] The objective is to train civilians who are competent in the specific themes of the various responsibilities involved in defense management and to provide them with the technical and administrative skills to interact with military personnel and state political officials

[2579] Given the limited local academic offerings for civilian defense training, the creation of institutions was promoted to train specialized civilian professionals equipped with the skills and knowledge to work in this field and lead it

[2580] The National Defense School is the main center for civilian training in this field and is undergoing a transformation process aimed at adapting its structure and academic offerings to effectively participate in an educational network serving defense in cooperation with national universities, research organizations (CONICET and similar organizations), and the university institutes of the Armed Forces

[2581] which have distance learning opportunities, and the Joint Chiefs of Staff through the Joint War College

[2582] Military intelligence has been a permanent activity in the historical development of nations due to the need to have the capacity to identify potential threats to their survival and development

[2583] Therefore, all States have agencies that perform these functions

[2584] Military Intelligence Civil defense governance also involves these activities in regard to the orientation and direction of the strategic, operational and tactical levels

[2585] However, in the past, military intelligence—used as an instrument of repression and coercion—had broad operational discretion, favoring the organizational fragmentation and self-governance of the various intelligence agencies

[2586] As a result, these structures, which were established to defend civil society, became a concrete threat to citizens

[2587] Since the restoration of democracy in 1983, the need arose to reorient the National Intelligence System toward full civilian leadership and thus address the identification of real and potential threats of external origin, emanating from the military instruments of state actors of interest

[2588] Likewise, the consolidation of the rule of law entailed other challenges for the sector, the main one being the need to find a fair balance between the principles of transparency and free access to public information (essential in a democratic regime) and the preservation of data with security classification (an inherent characteristic of intelligence systems

[2589] This situation has been overcome by identifying intelligence as a "subject subject to control" through the monitoring of its activities by civilian officials and, above all, by specific external oversight bodies composed of members of the National Congress

[2590] The aforementioned conversion also took place in a context of profound changes in intelligence production models, consolidating one based on knowledge

[2591] The digital revolution has enabled access to significant flows of information, available to both developed and developing countries

[2592] Taking advantage of this particular situation will depend on the intelligence systems' ability to channel this flow of data toward the objectives established by the National Government in this area

[2593] Within this framework, Argentina has achieved tangible transformations in military intelligence through the approval and promulgation of new regulatory instruments of various kinds that have allowed for the implementation of organizational, functional, doctrinal, and operational reforms

[2594] Likewise, this transformative process, which will be described later in this chapter, made it possible to modify the organizational culture of these organizations

[2595] The National Intelligence Law and Military Intelligence As described in previous chapters, the process of institutionalization of military intelligence began with the sanction of the National Defense Law in

[2596] This rule established, as one of its founding principles, the separation between defense and internal security, establishing in Article 15 that the domestic affairs of our country—whether public security or otherwise—could not, under any circumstances, be considered as working hypotheses for military intelligence agencies

[2597] This principle was reaffirmed in the Internal Security Act of

[2598] In 2001, the approval of the National Intelligence Law, with its respective regulations, established the legal, organic, and functional foundations of the National Intelligence System

[2599] It established the general principles that were to guide this public activity, as well as the system's limits, with special reference to the protection of the rights and guarantees of residents already recognized in the text of the National Constitution

[2600] The law also clearly established the missions and functions of the intelligence agencies of the Defense System, and created the Bicameral Commission for the Oversight of Intelligence Agencies and Activities within the National Congress

[2601] According to this legal instrument, the National Intelligence System (SIN) is composed of: Intelligence Secretariat: This is the highest body of the Intelligence System and directly reports organically to the Presidency of the Nation

[2602] It has the function of directing and coordinating the SIN

[2603] National Directorate of Criminal Intelligence: dependent on the Ministry of Justice, Security and Human Rights, its function is to produce criminal intelligence

[2604] National Directorate of Military Strategic Intelligence (DNIEM): dependent on the Ministry of Defense, its function is to produce military strategic intelligence

[2605] This Directorate's mission is also to guide, coordinate, direct, plan, and supervise activities related to intelligence production carried out by the Armed Forces' intelligence agencies at the operational and tactical levels

[2606] Based on the responsibilities assigned to each of the aforementioned agencies by Law No. 25,520, the following types of intelligence can be distinguished: National Intelligence: This is the activity consisting of obtaining, gathering, systematizing and analyzing specific information related to events, threats, risks and conflicts that affect the external and internal security of the Nation

[2607] Counterintelligence: is the activity within the field of intelligence that is carried out with the purpose of preventing intelligence activities by actors that represent threats or risks to the security of the National State

[2608] Criminal Intelligence: This is the branch of intelligence that addresses specific criminal activities that, due to their nature, magnitude, foreseeable consequences, danger, or methods, affect the freedom, life, and property of residents, their rights and guarantees, and the institutions of the representative, republican, and federal system established by the National Constitution

[2609] Military Strategic Intelligence: This is the branch of intelligence concerned with understanding the capabilities and weaknesses of the military potential of countries of interest from the perspective of national defense, as well as the geographic environment of the strategic operational areas determined by military strategic planning

[2610] National Directorate of Military Strategic Intelligence Intelligence Body of the Joint Chiefs of Staff of the Armed Forces

[2611] Army Intelligence Body Air Force Intelligence Body Navy Intelligence Body Produces military strategic intelligence DEFENSE INTELLIGENCE SUBSYSTEM Prepares Intelligence Plan Produces the strategic, operational and tactical intelligence necessary for planning and conducting operations

[2613] Transformation of the Military Intelligence Subsystem 3.1 Regulatory and Doctrinal Reform Despite the transformation implied by the approval of the National Intelligence Law, the autonomy and inorganic nature that the military intelligence agencies had acquired prevented them from operating in accordance with the provisions of current regulations, making it possible for them to continue carrying out some of the institutional practices that they had carried out for years

[2614] Therefore, it was crucial to move forward with the review and eventual modification of intelligence regulations, manuals, and plans (at all levels of military intelligence) to initiate a process of change in organizational culture

[2615] Within this framework, the following actions were established

[2616] The regulatory decree of the National Intelligence Law established in Article 6 that the National Directorate of Military Strategic Intelligence would coordinate the actions of the intelligence agencies of the Armed Forces, and would also be responsible for raising the area's budgetary requirements

[2617] In May 2003, a statute was approved for the Personnel of the Intelligence Secretariat and for the Civilian Intelligence Personnel of the Intelligence Agencies of the Armed Forces, institutionally establishing how professionals in this State function are recruited, trained, educated, promoted, dismissed, and/or retired

[2618] In accordance with the transparency guidelines established for this sector and in order to collaborate with the cases in which those responsible for state terrorism in the 1970s and 1980s are being tried, as well as with regard to the clarification of the terrorist attacks against the Israeli embassy and the AMIA mutual organization, intelligence officials were relieved of their obligation to maintain secrecy

[2619] Ministry of Defense Resolution No. 381/06 established that the subsystem's mission is to "assist the Minister of Defense in all intelligence-related matters necessary for the conduct of national defense affairs

[2620] It also established that the Military Intelligence Subsystem would be made up of "the set of intelligence agencies and departments of the Ministry of Defense and the intelligence agencies of the Armed Forces, functionally related for the purpose of producing Military Strategic Intelligence, Operational Strategic Intelligence, and Tactical Intelligence

[2621] A doctrinal review and adaptation of all matters relating to the intelligence of the Armed Forces was carried out, based on Ministerial Resolutions Nos. 386/06 and 699/06, which provided the political leadership with a tool for doctrinal training and the implementation of activities consistent with current legislation

[2622] Strategic Planning A further step in this transformation process was the implementation of the first Military Intelligence Plan

[2623] This activity begins with the assistance requested by CODENA (see chapter XV) to identify actors, situations and trends that, both at the regional and global levels, may be of interest to national defense

[2624] After conducting a thorough analysis and assessment of each of the contributions made by the participating state sectors, CODENA reports to the President of the Nation, describing the different scenarios and situations that may represent opportunities or potential risks to the achievement of national interests

[2625] Thus, the President has the necessary elements of judgment to establish the scenarios that correspond to national defense and intelligence

[2626] Guided by these strategic guidelines, the Intelligence Secretariat formulates the National Intelligence Plan, which specifies the needs that must be met by both the Defense Intelligence System and the other agencies that comprise the National Intelligence Service

[2627] Based on the actions taken at CODENA and within the framework of the National Defense Policy, the Ministry of Defense is developing its Intelligence Directive, through which it provides the DNIEM with the general guidelines that should guide the planning and production of intelligence for the entire subsystem

[2628] These documents enable the DNIEM, as the governing body, to initiate the Defense Intelligence Planning Cycle and develop the actions that direct and oversee activities at the national strategic (defense sector), military strategic, operational strategic, and tactical levels

[2629] The Planning Cycle then continues with the intervention of the Intelligence Unit of the Joint Chiefs of Staff of the Armed Forces (EMCO), to which the DNIEM establishes the policies, objectives, goals, and indicators that the Military Intelligence System must meet

[2630] Once the EMCO has identified the knowledge requirements of the higher level and its own, it directs and coordinates the participation of the Military Intelligence System in the Cycle by issuing a Military Intelligence Strategic Plan

[2631] In this way, it specifies which information needs are the responsibility of the Joint Operational Command, other commands and strategic areas considered in planning at the operational level and for each of the forces

[2632] This circumstance makes the EMCO intelligence body the coordinating body of the Military Intelligence Subsystem

[2633] The continuity of the Cycle is realized through the actions of the intelligence bodies of the Joint Operational Command and the General Staffs of each of the forces in their capacity as responsible for their own systems

[2634] These structures produce intelligence plans (at the strategic operational level) that determine the actions to be developed by each of the subordinate levels to produce the necessary knowledge (at the tactical level) and keep the components established for that level up to date

[2635] Finally, the Planning Cycle is completed with intelligence generation, which is the process through which the necessary actions are implemented to transform the data and information obtained into intelligence of interest to decision-making levels

[2636] This methodology was first implemented in 2007, when the DNIEM developed and implemented the first Strategic Plan for the Defense Intelligence System (PESID

[2637] This enabled the Cycle to move and the corresponding structures to develop and disseminate the plans that correspond to them

[2638] This is what the EMCO did with the Joint Staff Intelligence Plan (PIEMCO), and the Armed Forces with their specific plans

[2639] The Civilian Management of Military Intelligence The reform of the military intelligence subsystem requires controls that ensure the effectiveness, efficiency, and transparency of the actions of intelligence agencies

[2640] However, one of the serious difficulties in this field is the lack of civilians trained and educated in the management, production, and control of military strategic intelligence

[2641] In this regard, actions were taken to recruit and train analysts who had certified professional training and were also committed to democratic and republican values

[2642] This forced the DNIEM to initiate a specific training process through the National Intelligence School (ENI) and the Armed Forces Intelligence Institute (IIFA

[2643] Civilian management of defense intelligence matters is essential for the formation of structures that ensure the proper functioning of military intelligence agencies in this area

[2644] In accordance with the delegative attitude described in Chapter XII, when the direction and control at the higher levels of military intelligence matters are not covered by civilian officials with sufficient knowledge, experience and suitability, military intelligence itself fills this gap with its own cadres, acquiring inappropriate degrees of autonomy and self-government

[2645] For this reason, the training and formation of civilians constitutes a sine qua non condition for the effective exercise of political governance over military intelligence matters

[2646] In this regard, it is worth noting that in December 2005, the President of the Nation appointed the first civilian Director of the DNIEM, marking a milestone in the civilian leadership of the national defense intelligence subsystem

[2647] Army personnel with tactical intelligence equipment

[2648] The Future of Military Intelligence As described in Chapter XII, one of the greatest challenges of the consolidation of Argentine democracy was the establishment of civilian leadership of defense

[2649] Similarly, such management requires a clear legal framework for military intelligence and political and institutional control over its activities

[2650] On the other hand, the consolidation of the democratic transition process in Latin America and the progressive and consequent integration of the subcontinent also require an effort from the intelligence community

[2651] Within this framework, military intelligence in South America in particular, and in Latin America in general, must progressively adapt to the new scenario, moving beyond the outdated view of national defense organized around a framework of "regional interstate threats" toward a conception of defense as a "regional public good," in which states have growing needs for integration and complementarity

[2652] Consequently, beyond the marked evolution described, in pursuit of the consolidation of an effective, efficient military intelligence system consistent with democratic and republican values, elements are emerging that will warrant continued work in the near future on the same foundations and action strategies: - Continue developing systems that optimize coordination between the agencies involved and improve the current operational situation

[2653] Optimize the current educational offering to prioritize the activity's role in advising and assisting in decision-making

[2654] Interact more deeply with other structures to enhance the quality of knowledge required by a modern management system

[2655] Strengthen dialogue and cooperation with other defense intelligence agencies in the region as an ideal mechanism for strengthening mutual trust

[2656] Contribute to the regional overcoming of a planning framework based on "conflict hypothesis" and the consolidation of a model based on "confluence hypothesis and capacity planning," thereby contributing to reducing the gap between national and regional interests

[2657] Chapter XX HUMAN RIGHTS The protection and respect of human rights constitute a program of action in continuous implementation carried out at all levels of the Argentine State

[2658] This is the meaning of the set of obligations that the Argentine Republic assumed following the constitutional reform of 1994, which reinforced the national State's domestic and international commitment by prioritizing international instruments for the protection of these fundamental rights

[2659] This programmatic basis for the development of public policies is particularly relevant for countries like Argentina, which have experienced successive constitutional fractures in which the Armed Forces, among other sectors, have played a leading role

[2660] International Instruments for the Protection of Human Rights Incorporated into the Constitution Chapter Four: Powers of Congress Art

[2661] To approve or reject treaties concluded with other nations and with international organizations and concordats with the Holy See

[2662] Treaties and concordats have a higher hierarchy than laws

[2663] The American Declaration of the Rights and Duties of Man; the Universal Declaration of Human Rights; the American Convention on Human Rights; the International Covenant on Economic, Social and Cultural Rights; the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights and its Optional Protocol; the Convention on the Prevention and Punishment of the Crime of Genocide; the International Convention on the Elimination of All Forms of Racial Discrimination; the Convention on the Elimination of All Forms of Discrimination against Women; the Convention against Torture and Other Cruel, Inhuman or Degrading Treatment or Punishment; the Convention on the Rights of the Child; under the conditions of their validity, they have constitutional status, do not repeal any article of the first part of this Constitution, and must be understood as complementary to the rights and guarantees recognized herein

[2664] They may only be denounced, if applicable, by the National Executive Branch, with the prior approval of two-thirds of the total members of each Chamber

[2665] Other human rights treaties and conventions, once approved by Congress, will require a two-thirds vote of the total members of each House to enjoy constitutional status

[2666] In the first twenty years after the restoration of the democratic system, the issue of human rights—in relation to the defense sector in general and the Armed Forces in particular—focused on civil-military relations, the role of the Armed Forces in democracy, and their relationship with the bodies reviewing the recent dictatorial past

[2667] In this context, the Defense System, in its transformation process, incorporated a cross-cutting human rights policy as a tool for the modernization and professional strengthening of military institutions

[2668] These policies include: a) the review of regulations and practices that do not comply with national legislation and international instruments for the protection of human rights; b) active cooperation with the process of memory, truth, and justice to clarify human rights violations committed by the last dictatorship; c) the incorporation of a gender equity perspective

[2669] The institutionalization of human rights policy in the defense sector began in 2003 when the Executive Branch authorized the Ministry of Defense to "intervene in the implementation and dissemination of international humanitarian law and human rights law

[2670] In 2006, the National Directorate of Human Rights and International Humanitarian Law was created within the Ministry of Defense as a specific body responsible for the implementation, application, and dissemination of law in these areas, both in times of peace and conflict, in conjunction with the powers in this area corresponding to the Secretariat of Human Rights of the Ministry of Justice, Security and Human Rights of the Nation, and the Ministry of Foreign Affairs, International Trade and Worship

[2671] Objectives and lines of action The Ministry of Defense has set as its general objective the promotion of actions aimed at incorporating a human rights perspective as an indispensable tool in the process of institutional strengthening of the Armed Forces and for the construction of an institutional culture that aligns its missions, functions, and practices with the basic guidelines of a democratic state governed by the rule of law

[2672] The main lines of action followed were the following: a) Promotion of legal and regulatory reforms that are essential to adapt current regulations in the area of national defense to the requirements regarding the fundamental rights of individuals mandated by the National Constitution and the international instruments by which the Argentine State is bound

[2673] Development of a coordinated policy with other state agencies regarding memory, truth, and justice, through compliance with the duties of cooperation and diligence in the investigation of human rights violations that occurred during the rise of state terrorism in the 1970s and early 1980s

[2674] Implementation and sustainability of training, education, and dissemination initiatives on the subject, aimed at those involved in the field of national defense, whether through the advice required by the Ministry's competent areas in education, or by promoting the development of specific extracurricular activities aimed at fostering a perspective among citizens who choose the military profession that highlights their status as holders of fundamental rights

[2675] e) Development of a coordinated and centralized policy of action with other State agencies responsible for promoting policies of respect for rights, institutions and mechanisms for monitoring guarantees, such as the Secretariat of Human Rights of the Ministry of Justice of the Nation, the National Institute for Combating Discrimination, Xenophobia and Racism (INADI) and the Human Rights Directorate of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs, as well as with other similar State agencies at the provincial or local levels. [2676] Central Actions

[2677] Institutional Transformation Processes and Review of Regulations and Practices a) Measures to Protect the Human Rights of Members of the Armed Forces Elimination of discriminatory requirements based on purely aesthetic characteristics from the current regulations for entry into military institutions

[2678] As of November 2006, purely aesthetic requirements for admission to or continued service in military institutions were waived, as they bore no relation to the demands of military activity and represented an open form of discrimination

[2679] “One of the most important ways to promote substantive reforms within the Armed Forces is (…) for the current Armed Forces not to buy into or take responsibility for the heavy legacy of Armed Forces that have committed serious human rights violations

[2680] They are not responsible

[2681] The young people who serve in the Armed Forces today do not have to carry that legacy

[2682] And in that sense, it seems to me that an agenda that promotes democratic reforms and human rights policies within the Armed Forces is the best way to incorporate these democratic principles

[2683] Establishing a ban on any form of consultation on matters related to the religious beliefs of individuals serving in or aspiring to join military institutions

[2684] In June 2007, a practice that blatantly contradicts Argentina's policy on the protection of personal data revealing racial and ethnic origin, political opinions, religious, philosophical, or moral beliefs, union membership, and information relating to health or sexual life was eliminated

[2685] Elimination of the ban on marriage between Armed Forces personnel of different ranks or with members of the Security Forces

[2686] As of August 2007, all restrictions preventing marriage between military personnel of different ranks or with members of the Security Forces were eliminated for all three Armed Forces

[2687] This is because family law cannot be subject to regulations other than those established by law that affect the equal treatment of military personnel

[2688] Given its incompatibility with constitutional norms, it was also ordered that any sanctions imposed under the previous regulations be repealed

[2689] Elimination of existing directives in the Army and Air Force that collected information on so-called "regular and irregular family situations

[2690] In January 2008, the directives that, under the undue arrogation of the power to regulate aspects of the private lives of military personnel, required men and women of the Armed Forces to provide information about their family circumstances were repealed. This was aggravated by the fact that in cases that the authorities considered "irregular" or "special," this had consequences for their possibilities of professional development and continued military careers

[2691] Elimination of existing regulations in the Armed Forces that required authorization or permission from a superior officer as a requirement for marriage

[2692] The measure, in February 2008, eliminated existing regulations in the three Armed Forces requiring express superior authorization for marriage

[2693] Elimination of discrimination between biological, adopted, marital or extramarital children

[2694] In February 2008, the elimination of all types of discrimination regarding adopted children, biological children, children born through marriage, and children born out of wedlock was established, banishing stigmatizing norms that are contrary to the dignity of persons and their right to be treated under conditions of equality, as established by national legislation

[2695] Part III B) Measures to prevent the incorporation of personnel with a history of human rights violations Implementation and control of the procedure for the incorporation of retired military personnel ensuring the intervention of the National Secretariat of Human Rights

[2696] Considering that retired or discharged military personnel may perform duties in the various departments under the control of the Armed Forces, both under the regime provided for in Article 62 of Law 19.101 and under other ties, it was considered essential to ensure that the eventual incorporation of such personnel would comply with professional and ethical criteria and considerations for such a role

[2697] Incorporation of the requirement of not having a criminal record for human rights violations in the contracting documents of private security companies

[2698] Beginning in November 2007, Armed Forces commanders were instructed to incorporate, as a requirement for hiring private security and custody, the absence of records linked to human rights violations in the National Memory Archive of the National Secretariat of Human Rights

[2699] In this way, the requirements of the specifications were adapted to those established in national regulations, which establish the standards for the authorization of natural or legal persons requesting authorization to provide private security and custody services throughout the country

[2700] Policies of Memory, Truth and Justice 2.2.a Coordination of actions with government authorities in the context of cases of serious human rights violations involving national defense personnel Following the enactment of Law 25.77913 and the decision of the Supreme Court of Justice of the Nation in the case "Simón, Julio Héctor and others s/unlawful deprivation of liberty", cases of human rights violations were reopened

[2702] Thus, it was ordered that the heads of the Armed Forces assign urgent and preferential status to all judicial documents and requests from government agencies in the context of cases involving serious human rights violations

[2703] Since 2007, there has been a sustained increase in such requests, going from just over one hundred documents processed in 2007 to four hundred during 2008 and around six hundred in 2009, all originating from different jurisdictions of the Federal Justice or the Public Prosecutor's Office of the Nation

[2773] Part III Chapter XXI Gender Perspective and Equity The goal of generating better conditions of equity between women and men in defense institutions has been implemented in various actions that revolve around issues of professional relationships, the possibility of access and permanence under conditions of equal treatment; to which is added a program aimed at banishing discriminatory practices and other forms of gender violence

[2774] The Entry of Women into the Armed Forces Even with specific cases, women were already present in the military campaigns of the South American emancipation of the 19th century

[2775] As the historian Lily Sosa de Newton points out in “Women in the Argentine Armies”, in those early times the personalities of, among other heroines, General Juana Azurduy de Padilla, Ensign Manuela Pedraza and María Remedios del Valle, a poor black woman who, due to her merits in the defense against the English invasions, obtained the rank of cavalry sergeant major, and was promoted to captain by Manuel Belgrano by virtue of her performance in the Army of the North, stood out

[2776] But it wasn't until the 1980s that the process of opening up the ranks of the Argentine Armed Forces to women began, a process that would be completed twenty years later, at the beginning of the 21st century

[2777] Until those years, military personnel had been composed exclusively of men, and only women had been performing civil administrative, auxiliary, technical, or professional tasks since the middle of the last century

[2778] The entry of women for military performance begins in the professional corps of the noncommissioned officers of the Navy, the Army and the Air Force

[2779] The next stage is the incorporation of women into the command corps

[2780] In the non-commissioned officer ranks of the three forces, the Navy does so simultaneously with entry into the professional corps, and a decade and a half later, the Army and the Air Force

[2781] During that decade, in 1992, the first female candidates for military officer ranks were allowed with the creation of the Military School for Combat Support Services Officers (EMCFASC) in the Army. In 1997, the National Military College opened the door for female candidates to join command corps

[2782] The Air Force did so in 2001 by opening admission to the Military Aviation School, and the Navy in 2002 by opening admission to the Military Naval School

[2783] Currently, there are only restrictions on female performance in the command corps of the Army's Infantry and Cavalry branches for female volunteer soldiers

[2784] In Dora Barrancos and others, Women and their struggles in Argentine history, Ministry of Defense of the Argentine Republic, Buenos Aires, 216 p. Due to her performance in the battle of Villar, Juana Azurduy de Padilla received the rank of lieutenant colonel granted by Supreme Director Pueyrredón

[2785] In July 2009, President Cristina Fernández de Kirchner posthumously promoted her to the rank of general

[2792] The participation of Women in Military Personnel Qualification Bodies The qualification of personnel, to determine promotions and discharges, is the responsibility of Qualification Boards whose composition is determined by the different regulations of the Armed Forces

[2793] To encourage the participation of women, a decree was issued ordering the chiefs of the general staffs of each armed force to include in the different instances of the Qualification Boards of senior and junior personnel, female military personnel who are in the ranks to be considered for the integration of said boards

[2794] The regulation stipulates that until active female commando personnel reach the required ranks, their inclusion will be without prejudice to the corps, branch, and/or rank to which they belong

[2795] Until this reform, there was no record of women participating in the Army and Air Force Qualification Boards

[2796] In the case of the Navy, only the Qualification Board for non-commissioned officers had included female soldiers

[2797] Women in Peacekeeping Missions The United Nations peacekeeping missions have facilitated the recognition and full exercise of equal professional rights for women in military service

[2798] The Argentine Republic has implemented initiatives aimed at recognizing gender perspectives in this area, including the United Nations "Action Plan for the Implementation of the Gender Perspective in Peacekeeping Operations

[2799] This is a cross-cutting policy for promoting gender perspectives, characterized by active dissemination—through seminars and publications—and consistent actions

[2800] The following are noteworthy: - Participation, through voluntary application, in the development of a pilot plan for the national implementation of United Nations Security Council Resolution 1325/2000, which seeks to implement projects aimed at materializing the guidelines issued by the world organization on the matter

[2801] Creation in 2008 of the Working Group for the diagnosis and analysis of measures and actions for the effective implementation of gender perspectives within the framework of peacekeeping operations

[2802] The integration of women in the Argentine contingents deployed in United Nations peacekeeping missions places Argentina as a nation close to the top ten in terms of the number of women deployed in recent years

[2803] Since 1993, 341 women have been members of the Armed Forces

[2804] have participated in peace missions

[2805] Of these, 68.7% did so in the last ten years

[2806] Meanwhile, 58.8% of them worked in health care areas, while the rest performed other operational tasks

[2807] Action Plan to Implement the Gender Perspective in Peace Operations In July 2007 in the city of Pretoria (South Africa), Argentina was chosen by the United Nations Department of Peacekeeping Operations (DPKO) to develop a pilot plan for the implementation of Security Council Resolution

[2831] Gender Policy Council This Council, created in 2007, was conceived as an advisory body to the Minister of Defense, seeking to ensure the active participation of military women who, in the first survey, had demanded a better representation position

[2833] The Council has a diverse composition, with the participation of women from the three Armed Forces, civil society organizations, university academic institutes, and various state agencies

[2834] The areas of work that have been consolidated include, among other topics, family life and motherhood, the issue of leadership relationships and abuse of authority, occupational issues related to working conditions, prevention and response mechanisms for abuse of power and violence, career regulations, and women's participation in decision-making

[2895] Part III Chapter XXII JUSTICE SYSTEM One of the main transformations in the legal framework of the Armed Forces was the comprehensive reform of its disciplinary system, a system that, governed by an old Code of Military Justice, did not correspond to current national legislation and international regulations

[2896] Nor was it consistent with the political concepts and guidelines for national defense in a democratic state governed by the rule of law

[2897] This system and code had already been challenged before the Inter-American Commission on Human Rights (IACHR) for contradicting international standards for the protection of human rights, especially those that constitute guarantees of due process, liberty, and human dignity

[2898] Within the framework of a friendly settlement, the Argentine government then assumed responsibility before the IACHR for promoting a reform that included the active participation of representatives from academia, the military, and civil society

[2899] At the request of the Executive Branch and based on the recommendations of the commission of experts convened by the Ministry of Defense, in August 2008 the National Congress passed Law 26,394, which repealed the Military Justice Code (Law 14,029); amended the National Penal and Criminal Procedure Codes; established a Military Criminal Procedure Code for times of war or other armed conflicts and Instructions for the civilian population; a Code of Discipline for the Armed Forces; and a Joint Justice Service for the Armed Forces

[2900] Some of the most important aspects are: - The treatment of military crimes within the jurisdiction of the Federal Justice of the Nation, eliminating what was called military jurisdiction for the prosecution of crimes committed by members of the Armed Forces

[2901] The elimination of the death penalty from the Argentine legal system, which, although not in use, remained in force in the military sphere

[2902] The complete redesign of the disciplinary system, in order to ensure that the sanctioned conduct and the procedures for doing so are adapted to the needs of the service's effectiveness and ensure the value of discipline as such, but with full adherence to the rights and guarantees established by the Constitution of the Argentine Nation and the international instruments for the protection of human rights (of constitutional hierarchy by virtue of the provisions of article 75, paragraph 22 of our Magna Carta

[2903] The establishment of a single Joint Justice Service of the Armed Forces that records cases and provides assistance to members of any of the forces who are brought before the nation's courts

[2904] With this reform, the country left behind a long period in which its legislation granted fewer guarantees to the Argentine military in times of peace than to enemy prisoners in times of war

[2905] BASES FOR THE REFORM The immediate antecedent that founded the reform of the justice administration system in the military sphere was the friendly settlement agreement signed on August 14, 2006 between the Argentine Republic and the petitioning parties before the Inter-American Commission on Human Rights in case 11,758 (Rodolfo Correa Belisle

[2906] To this end, an ad hoc commission was established, comprising representatives of civil society organizations, academic units, and state and international agencies interested in Military Justice Reform

[2907] For its work – it lasted six months – the Principles on the Administration of Justice by Military Tribunals adopted by the United Nations in August 2005 were established as a guide and normative and doctrinal developments that had taken place in the country over the last twenty years of democracy were considered

[2908] The texts were submitted for comment and debate: first, they were made available to the legal services of the Joint Chiefs of Staff and each of the Armed Forces, who forwarded their opinions to the Ministry of Defense

[2909] Given the importance of the opinion of the military sector as a central actor 1- Resolution No. 154/2006. 2- The participating institutions of the Commission and their representatives were: - Faculty of Law of the University of Buenos Aires: Dr. Raúl Zaffaroni - Institute of Comparative Studies in Criminal and Social Sciences: Dr. Alberto Binder - Association of Women Judges of Argentina: Dr. Mirta López González - Center for Legal and Social Studies: Dr. Gastón Chillier - Center for the Implementation of Public Policies for Equity and Growth: Dr. Diego Friedman - International Committee of the Red Cross: Dr. Gabriel Vallardes - Planning Directorate of the General Staff of the Army: General of Justice Manuel Lozano - General Audit Office of the Armed Forces: Clte

[2910] José Agustín Reilly - Secretariat of Criminal Policy of the Ministry of Justice and Human Rights: Dr. Alejandro Slokar - Secretariat of Human Rights of the Ministry of Justice and Human Rights: Dr. Rodolfo Mattarollo

[2911] UN Document E/CN

[2912] Part III of the change provided for a day of debate and discussion on the proposed texts, mainly the Disciplinary Code and the Criminal Procedure for Times of War, in which one hundred officers from the three Armed Forces participated

[2913] Secondly, the projects were submitted for consultation with academics and civil society organizations for a month, inviting them to participate with comments

[2914] The exchange modality generated truly valuable contributions for the final review
