[2920] AXES OF THE REFORM Two essential concepts prevailed in the reform: one, that there can be no rules governing the performance of members or officials of a state institution that are not in accordance with the Constitution of the Nation; and the other, that within this framework, to strengthen the quality of the Armed Forces as institutions of a democratic state governed by the rule of law, it was essential to adapt their rules and procedures

[2921] The previous model, governed by the Military Code in force since 1951, established for citizens of military profession rules and a system of judgment and administration of sentences that contradicted the constitutional system of the Judicial Branch of the Nation, lacked guarantees for due process and respect for the principles of publicity and "contradictoriness" - it was disconnected from national and international legal instruments for the protection of human rights - and even in the treatment of minor disciplinary matters it proceeded with extreme bureaucratic delay without the possibility of review and with sanctions that deprived liberty that could extend up to a period of six months

[2922] Making the points set out above more explicit: a. Treatment of essentially military crimes within the jurisdiction of the Federal Justice of the Nation

[2923] Military jurisdiction was eliminated for the prosecution of crimes committed by members of the Armed Forces

[2924] This safeguards the procedural guarantees of independence, impartiality, and equality of military professionals who could be reasonably suspected of having committed crimes

[2925] This innovation assumes that the recognition of the principles that inform common criminal law must also apply to citizens with a military profession

[2926] b. Elimination of the death penalty from the Argentine legal system

[2927] The death penalty, although not used, remained in force in the military sphere

[2928] Its elimination is not a mere formality but a step forward in deepening the democratic state's commitment to people, to their integrity and dignity

[2929] Furthermore, the elimination removes the risk that the death penalty—formally legitimized by its existence in the legal system—could be used at some point

[2930] c. Elimination of the courts of honor

[2931] Law 26.394 eliminated the so-called “honor courts” established in Argentina in the early 19th century, originating in Spanish military traditions and regulated by provisions of the de facto government of Alejandro A. Lanusse since

[2932] These courts were only competent to judge the “moral conduct of officers”, establishing 4- Law 19.101/1971, on Military Personnel

[2933] Chapter XXII 369 Part III establishing that violations of honor are “all acts and omissions attributable to officers that harm their own honor, or that of others, and affect the ethical heritage of military institutions and the military profession and its traditions.”

[2934] The courts of honor could punish those who, for the same offense, had been deemed innocent by a civilian judge or even by the military disciplinary system, thus contradicting one of the general principles of law that prohibits double jeopardy for the same offense

[2935] d. Complete redesign of the disciplinary system

[2936] In this regard, the reform involved, as already indicated, adapting definitions and procedures to the needs of service efficiency, but, above all, to the requirements of the National Constitution (Article 18) and international instruments for the protection of human rights

[2937] In this way, the value of military discipline was ensured and rules that favored bureaucracy and arbitrariness were eliminated

[2938] To this end, the objectives of disciplinary control were clearly established, as well as their relationship to the needs of the services and functions of military activity

[2939] Thus, concepts that considered disciplinary structures as abstract guardians of the hierarchical nature of organizations, without any connection to the real need for discipline and its effectiveness, were overcome

[2940] Reorganization of justice services in the military sphere

[2948] In the exercise of disciplinary actions, the following are prohibited: Using disciplinary power to order or encourage tasks or actions unrelated to military functions

[2949] Sanction political, religious or moral ideas or beliefs

[2950] Affecting personal dignity, causing ridicule or humiliation, deliberately undermining self-esteem, or weakening team spirit and teamwork

[2951] Promote all forms of discrimination, as established in the respective laws

[2952] Conducting campaigns of personal or group harassment or promoting hatred and resentment between groups or units

[2953] Weaken personal and group capabilities that allow for the efficient completion of assigned tasks

[2954] Promote the discredit of inferiors or the weakening of the hierarchical order

[2955] Omitting the sanction of faults, which, although they do not produce an immediate effect, weaken the general state of discipline, except for express reasons of efficiency in the service

[2956] The application of sanctions with excessive rigor, formalism, or without any benefit to the fulfillment of tasks or the state of discipline

[2958] Chapter XXII 373 Part III Chapter XXIII WELL-BEING The well-being of personnel and their access to social rights constitutes one of the axes that make up the professionalization of the Armed Forces and the proper functioning of the Defense System

[2959] The transformation initiated in this area extends to the areas of health, access to housing, maternity and childhood, and pensions and retirement

[2960] The social security subsystem also includes personnel from the National Gendarmerie and the Naval Prefecture, since at the time of their creation these security forces depended on the Army and Navy respectively

[2961] Health According to the definition of the World Health Organization, a “Health System comprises the set of people, organizations and resources, as well as the rules that regulate them, that are dedicated to producing Health actions, that is, actions whose primary purpose is the promotion, prevention, recovery and rehabilitation of health.”

[2962] Within this conception, the Armed Forces Health System comprises two well-defined subsystems: the military health subsystem and the Armed Forces social security subsystem

[2963] While both share very similar objectives, they differ in some characteristics, mainly related to their sources of funding and the target population they serve

[2964] The military health subsystem provides healthcare services for active military and civilian personnel, and its source of funding is the national budget

[2965] The Armed Forces' social security subsystem provides health coverage and social benefits for all Armed Forces personnel, including family members, retirees, and pensioners

[2966] This subsystem is financed by contributions from members and contributions from the employer (the State

[2967] Each of these subsystems is described in the following sections

[2981] DIAGNOSIS OF HEALTH SUBSYSTEMS AT THE BEGINNING OF THIS DECADE Military health care in the three Armed Forces was showing significant deterioration, the main characteristics and causes of which were: - A high degree of fragmentation and lack of complementarity between the health services of the three forces; - Significant underutilization of the capacity of their health facilities; - Lack of investment and medium- and long-term planning, resulting in building deterioration, infrastructure failures, and outdated equipment; - Multiple funders and providers in hospital facilities; - Absence of a uniform list of benefits; - Restrictions on purchasing, contracting, and billing mechanisms, with a lack of centralization and cost and production measurement programs; - Insufficient quality policies for benefits; - Lack of a uniform human resources policy: coexistence of different employment regimes with different salaries and obligations for similar positions and salary gaps with market rates; staff shortages in numerous areas; - Deficient management control and IT systems; - The Joint Laboratory of the Armed Forces. [3080] Chapter XXIII 387 Part III Chapter XXIV ENVIRONMENTAL POLICY The National Constitution in its article 41 establishes that the inhabitants of the Nation enjoy the right to a healthy environment

[3081] It also imposes the duty to preserve it, assigning to the authorities the obligation to protect this right, verifying the rational use of natural resources and providing for the protection of biological diversity

[3082] The Argentine State has under its jurisdiction a significant extension of land assigned for use and administration to the Ministry of Defense, the Armed Forces, and other agencies in the defense sector

[3083] In compliance with current national regulations and international commitments, the Ministry of Defense has adopted an environmentally responsible approach to military activities

[3084] In this regard, it has designed and implemented an environmental policy based on the concept of sustainable development that is compatible with the primary and subsidiary missions of the Armed Forces

[3085] This policy is aimed at preserving, conserving, restoring, and improving the quality of environmental resources, both natural and cultural, while preserving the conduct of military activities on these lands

[3086] Over the past few decades, military use of these lands has, in many cases, contributed to ensuring the conservation of existing ecosystems through a permanent military presence, the enforcement of regulations regarding land security, and the design and implementation of the aforementioned environmental policy

[3087] The main pillars of the Ministry of Defense's environmental policy are: - Strict compliance with national and international regulations, that is, with those international conventions to which our country is a signatory

[3088] Incorporation of the concept of environmental damage prevention into the planning phase of all military training, maneuver, and instruction activities

[3089] Conservation, protection and restoration (where possible) of the 388 natural and cultural resources on the land assigned for use and administration by the Ministry of Defense and the Armed Forces

[3090] Promoting the commitment and participation of all levels of National Defense in reducing the risk of environmental damage

[3091] Interjurisdictional cooperation with national agencies related to environmental issues

[3092] Inclusion of adequate conceptual, legal, and operational preparation related to environmental issues in the training of both officers and non-commissioned officers

[3093] Argentina is a signatory to several international conventions related to environmental conservation: - Convention on Biological Diversity (approved by Law No. 24,375) - Millennium Declaration (UNITED NATIONS GENERAL ASSEMBLY Resolution No. 55/2) - Latin American and Caribbean Initiative for Sustainable Development (developed at the World Summit on Sustainable Development, held in Johannesburg, South Africa, 2002) In 1999, the Ministry of Defense decided to fully commit to the national environmental policy and implement the necessary actions to minimize the environmental impact produced by the usual activities of the Armed Forces and other dependent agencies

[3094] In this context, the Environmental Preservation Commission for Defense was created at the ministerial level, aimed at designing policies, plans and programs for environmental protection and preservation

[3095] Likewise, through a Ministerial Resolution, the objectives and main guidelines of the Ministry of Defense in environmental matters were defined

[3096] Following these guidelines, the Armed Forces have adopted measures geared toward environmentally responsible behavior, incorporating standards consistent with these objectives into their procedures

[3097] In 2007, and in order to unite the efforts of the different departments of the National State, the Ministry of Defense signed a Framework Agreement for Cooperation with the National Parks Administration in order to jointly design and implement active policies on in situ biodiversity conservation, through the identification of properties assigned for use by the Ministry of Defense that

[3098] Resolution MD

[3099] Part III could constitute Natural Areas of Conservation Interest (ENIC), either due to their original natural characteristics; because they host natural environments and a population of flora and fauna that in many cases is of high representative value and even unique to the region in which they are located (as a result of strong transformation processes in their surroundings); because they border other protected areas, thus acquiring a buffer value independent of their natural values; and because they contain examples of natural environments of intrinsic and/or educational value near urban areas

[3100] Within the framework of the aforementioned agreement, the biodiversity values of a series of federal properties assigned for use and management to the Ministry of Defense were certified, formulating and promoting their declaration as Natural Areas of Conservation Interest, all without prejudice to the military activity to which they are assigned

[3101] Through the signing of Additional Protocols between the National Parks Administration and the corresponding Armed Forces, those properties where certain biodiversity values and compatibility with the assigned military activity were verified and certified were declared Military Nature Reserves

Official site White Paper 2010 Within the framework of the reflection and consultation process “Building the Bicentennial White Paper”, the official website of the 2010 White Paper on Defense was developed: www.libroblanco2010.gob.ar as a tool that serves the following purposes: • To provide information on the process of drafting and discussing the White Paper through videos, photos, transcripts, and reference materials on the various activities carried out throughout this cycle; • To serve as another forum for discussion, reflection, and contributions both to the White Paper itself and to the discussion process; • To serve as an information space for all researchers and those interested in defense issues in general and White Papers in particular

[3164] To this end, it dynamically provides the majority of White Papers published to date, academic works, links to institutions involved in defense studies, among other resources; • It serves as a mechanism for disseminating the White Paper once it is published

[3165] Workshop activities methodology: After the speakers' presentations, a round of questions and answers takes place

[3166] Based on their presentations, attendees are divided into groups to discuss the main points of the proposed topic with a moderator

[3167] Finally, a report is prepared on what was discussed

[3168] In the case of Workshop III, the dynamics of the event were different; three presentations were made on different topics, which were presented by experts, and then a round of discussion was opened among all those present

[3169] After the three debates concluded, a report was given by professors from different universities. Seminars: The speakers' presentations were held around various thematic panels

[3170] At the end of each table, there is a round of questions and answers
